case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Confrontation Clause permits using a screen to block a child witness’s view of the defendant without the trial court making a case-specific, individualized finding that the procedure is necessary to prevent trauma to that particular child.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. VI (Confrontation Clause), as applied to Mississippi’s mandatory child-witness screen procedure (Miss. Code Ann. § 99-43-101(2)(g) is referenced in the record excerpts).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Pitts argues the trial court used a screen because Mississippi law mandated it, not because the judge made the individualized, on-the-record necessity finding required by Coy v. Iowa and Maryland v. Craig. Under those cases, the State must present case-specific evidence that this particular child would suffer serious trauma from seeing the defendant and that the screen is necessary; a legislative or generalized presumption of trauma is unconstitutional. Pitts emphasizes the record allegedly shows no such evidence (and even testimony that the child loved/missed him), so the procedure violated face-to-face confrontation. He further contends the Mississippi Supreme Court’s harmless-error reasoning is improper in this context and that the error warrants summary reversal because it directly conflicts with controlling Supreme Court precedent.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Mississippi argues the confrontation right’s essential purposes were satisfied because the child testified under oath, was subject to cross-examination, and was observable by the jury, and the trial court concluded the screen was necessary to protect the child from trauma. The State also stresses that any error was harmless beyond a reasonable doubt given overwhelming independent evidence of guilt, including multiple witness accounts of the child’s disclosures and a videotaped forensic interview admitted at trial (including that Pitts himself introduced), and therefore the case is a poor vehicle for Supreme Court review.
key_precedents: Ohio v. Roberts, 448 U.S. 56 (1980) (abrogated on other grounds by Crawford)

John Roberts.reasoning: The State’s strongest contention is that the screen preserved cross-examination and jury observation, so the Confrontation Clause’s functional aims were met. But as Justice Alito and Justice Kagan underscore, Craig makes those functional considerations relevant only after the trial court first makes an on-the-record, case-specific finding of necessity grounded in evidence about this particular child; a statutory default cannot substitute for that predicate. Coy treats a physical barrier as a core denial of face-to-face confrontation, and the record here indicates the screen was used because Mississippi law “mandated” it rather than because the judge found necessity for this witness. On narrow grounds, we should vacate and remand for application of the proper Craig framework, without opining more broadly on permissible child-witness protections when the required findings are actually made.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The State’s strongest contention—that oath, cross-examination, and jury observation of demeanor preserved the “essential purposes” of confrontation—mistakes Craig’s structure and invites the very sort of freewheeling balancing the Sixth Amendment does not permit. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, the constitutional baseline is face-to-face confrontation, and Coy treats a physical barrier as a paradigmatic denial of that right absent a narrowly justified exception. Craig allows that departure only upon an on-the-record, case-specific finding of necessity grounded in evidence about this particular child; a mandatory statutory default supplies no such predicate and cannot displace the defendant’s procedural entitlement. Because the State did not carry its burden to establish necessity before abridging face-to-face confrontation, the conviction rests on a Confrontation Clause violation, with harmlessness (if any) for the lower court to assess on remand under the proper framework.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The State’s strongest contention—that oath, cross-examination, and jury observation preserved the Confrontation Clause’s core functions—misunderstands Craig’s structure: those functional considerations come into play only after the trial court makes the predicate, case-specific necessity finding for dispensing with face-to-face confrontation. As the Chief Justice explains, the record suggests the screen was employed as a statutory default, and that cannot substitute for an on-the-record determination supported by evidence about this particular child, as Coy and Craig require. Accepting generalized legislative presumptions would, as Justice Kagan warns, erase Craig’s limiting principle and effectively authorize routine dilution of confrontation in criminal trials. On narrow grounds, vacatur and remand to apply Craig’s individualized framework is the appropriate disposition.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The State’s strongest rejoinder is that cross-examination occurred and the jury could observe demeanor, so the screen served only as a modest procedural accommodation for child protection. But as I understand Coy and Craig—and as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize—the Constitution requires a case-specific, on-the-record necessity finding before the State may dispense with face-to-face confrontation; a mandatory, statute-driven screen regime is not a mere regulation of how the right is asserted, it is a substantive carve-out from what evidence may be admitted without full confrontation. Permitting generalized legislative assumptions about trauma to substitute for individualized findings would revive the very reliability/necessity balancing Crawford rejects, replacing the Sixth Amendment’s prescribed procedure (confrontation) with judicial or legislative judgments about sufficiency. On this record, the absence of the Craig predicate findings is dispositive; harmlessness cannot supply the missing constitutionally required procedure.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The State’s best point is the functional one: cross-examination occurred and the jury could assess demeanor, so confrontation’s reliability aims were largely served. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, Craig makes that functional adequacy relevant only after a threshold, case-specific necessity finding on the record; here the screen appears to have been deployed as a statutory default, which is exactly the categorical approach Coy and Craig forbid. Allowing a legislature to replace the required individualized judicial determination with a classwide presumption would erase the limiting principle and invite routine dilution of face-to-face confrontation. The narrow, workable disposition is vacatur and remand for application of Craig (with harmless-error assessed, if appropriate, under the correct standard).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point is the functional one: cross-examination occurred, the witness testified under oath, and the jury could observe demeanor—so the screen did not defeat confrontation’s “essential purposes.” But as the Chief Justice stresses, Coy and Craig treat face-to-face confrontation as the constitutional baseline, and Craig permits departure only upon a case-specific, on-the-record finding of necessity supported by evidence about this particular child; a mandatory statutory default cannot substitute for that constitutional predicate. Allowing generalized legislative assumptions to do the work would effectively create a new categorical exception untethered to any close historical analogue and inconsistent with the Sixth Amendment’s fixed scope. Given the absence of the required individualized finding in this record, the violation is established, leaving harmless-error (if any) for proper application on remand.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The State’s strongest point is that the defendant retained core confrontation features—oath, cross-examination, and jury observation of demeanor—so requiring an explicit necessity finding would be an extra procedural formality. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, Craig makes the individualized, evidence-based necessity determination the constitutional predicate for dispensing with face-to-face confrontation; without that predicate, the State has not justified abridging the right itself, and a categorical statutory default cannot substitute for the required case-specific showing. This is not a free-floating, judge-made “best practice” but a condition our precedent imposed for the narrow Craig exception. On these narrow grounds, the absence of a case-specific necessity finding tied to this child establishes a Sixth Amendment violation, with harmless-error (if any) for remand.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The State’s strongest point is functional: cross-examination occurred and the jury could observe demeanor, so confrontation’s “essential purposes” were served. But as the Chief Justice explains, Coy makes face-to-face confrontation the baseline, and Craig permits departure only after an on-the-record, case-specific necessity finding grounded in evidence about this child—something a mandatory statutory default cannot supply. Treating a categorical legislative judgment as a substitute would collapse Craig’s limiting principle and effectively convert a constitutional guarantee into an evidentiary-management choice. On this record, the absence of the Craig predicate is dispositive, with any harmless-error analysis left for remand under the proper framework.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The State’s strongest argument is functional—that cross-examination occurred and the jury could observe demeanor, so the “essential purposes” of confrontation were satisfied despite the screen. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Craig permits this departure from the face-to-face baseline only after an on-the-record, case-specific necessity finding grounded in evidence about this particular child; a statute-driven default cannot substitute for that constitutional predicate. Treating “essential purposes” as sufficient without the Craig finding would invert the baseline/exception structure and invite doctrinal erosion by converting a narrow exception into a categorical carve-out. Because the Government did not carry its burden to justify the deviation in this case, the Confrontation Clause violation is established, and purported cures or harmlessness cannot supply the missing predicate.

John Roberts.reasoning: Coy and Craig make the threshold question dispositive: whether the trial court made an on-the-record, case-specific finding—based on evidence—that blocking this particular child’s view of the defendant was necessary to prevent trauma caused by the defendant’s presence. On this record, the screen appears to have been employed because Mississippi law mandated it, which functions as an impermissible categorical presumption rather than the individualized necessity determination Craig requires. Applying a narrow-grounds approach, that failure to conduct the required inquiry resolves the Confrontation Clause issue without reaching broader questions about the general validity of child-witness protections. Because the procedure directly eliminated face-to-face confrontation without the constitutionally required predicate findings, the judgment should be vacated for application of the proper Craig framework.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause’s text secures a right to confrontation, and this Court has recognized that its ordinary operation includes face-to-face confrontation at trial. Under Coy, a screen that blocks the child witness’s view of the defendant is a paradigmatic denial of that face-to-face encounter, and Craig permits such a departure only upon a case-specific, on-the-record finding of necessity grounded in evidence that this particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence. Here, the trial court used the screen because Mississippi law mandated it and the record, as described, lacks the individualized necessity finding Coy and Craig require; generalized legislative assumptions about trauma cannot substitute for that constitutional predicate. Because the procedure altered the mode of confrontation itself without the required case-specific justification, it violated the Sixth Amendment as construed in Craig and Coy.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Sixth Amendment’s text guarantees the accused the right “to be confronted with the witnesses against him,” and this Court has treated face-to-face confrontation as the baseline rule. Under Coy and Craig, any departure from that rule requires an on-the-record, case-specific finding—based on evidence—that this particular child would suffer serious trauma from seeing the defendant and that the chosen measure is necessary; a mandatory or generalized legislative presumption cannot substitute for that individualized judicial determination. Here, the record as described indicates the screen was employed because Mississippi law mandated it, not because the trial judge made the required individualized necessity finding tied to this child, which is a straightforward conflict with controlling precedent. Even crediting the State’s strong interest in protecting children and its harmless-error arguments, allowing a categorical rule would invite routine dilution of confrontation rights in criminal cases and is precisely what Coy and Craig forbid.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Sixth Amendment guarantees confrontation as a procedure—face-to-face accusation and cross-examination—not an ad hoc judicial (or legislative) judgment that the evidence is "reliable enough." Under Coy and Craig, a court may depart from face-to-face confrontation for a child witness only upon a case-specific, individualized, on-the-record finding that this particular child would suffer serious trauma from seeing the defendant and that the chosen measure is necessary; a mandatory, statute-driven screen regime functions as an impermissible substantive carve-out from the confrontation right rather than a reasonable procedural regulation of how it is invoked. On these facts, the screen was used because Mississippi law purportedly mandated it, and the record as described contains no individualized necessity showing tied to this child’s ability to testify in the defendant’s presence, making the procedure constitutionally defective under our confrontation framework. The State’s fallback to “essential purposes” and harmlessness cannot supply the missing constitutionally required procedure, because the Clause demands the proper method of testing testimony—confrontation—before the State may secure conviction with that testimony.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Coy and Craig make the Sixth Amendment’s face-to-face component the default, and permit departures only when the trial court makes an on-the-record, case-specific finding—after hearing evidence—that this particular child needs the protection to avoid serious trauma. On this record, the screen appears to have been used as a mandatory statutory routine rather than as a tailored, judicially found necessity, which is the kind of categorical presumption Craig rejected as inconsistent with the Clause’s design. A workable, coherent Confrontation Clause rule cannot allow legislatures to displace the individualized judicial determination Craig requires, because that would erase the constitutional limiting principle and invite inconsistent administration across cases. Whatever the strength of the State’s harmlessness arguments, the Mississippi Supreme Court’s rule upholding screen use without the Craig findings conflicts with controlling precedent and undermines the statutory-purpose/workability compromise Craig struck between child protection and confrontation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Sixth Amendment’s confrontation guarantee, as originally understood, secured a defendant’s right to meet adverse witnesses “face to face,” admitting only historically established exceptions—and the State identifies no founding-era analogue allowing a categorical, legislatively presumed denial of that encounter for an entire class of witnesses. Under this Court’s controlling decisions, Coy held a screen that blocks a child’s view of the accused is a paradigmatic confrontation violation, and Craig tolerated a departure only upon a case-specific, on-the-record finding of necessity grounded in evidence about this particular child. Here the screen was employed as a mandatory statutory default, without the individualized necessity determination Coy and Craig demand, so the procedure cannot be sustained by appeals to generalized policy concerns or broad “purposes” like protecting children. Because the trial court failed to make the required record-based finding before restricting face-to-face confrontation, the judgment rests on a constitutional error under our settled framework.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Coy and Craig recognize a substantive Sixth Amendment right to face-to-face confrontation, and they allow departures only when the trial court makes a case-specific finding of necessity grounded in evidence that this particular child would be traumatized by seeing the defendant and that the chosen measure is necessary. Mississippi’s screen procedure, as applied here, appears to have been triggered by the statute’s mandatory “right” to a screen rather than by an individualized, on-the-record determination tied to this child—precisely the kind of generalized, legislatively presumed justification that Coy and Craig reject. My usual reluctance to impose extra procedural requirements does not control because Craig itself expressly demands a case-specific necessity determination before the State may abridge face-to-face confrontation, and federalism does not permit a State to dispense with that required safeguard by statute. On this record, the State has not shown with particularized support that use of this screen for this child was necessary, so the Confrontation Clause violation is established (leaving harmless-error to be assessed under the proper standard on remand).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause’s founding-era core was face-to-face confrontation, and this Court’s precedents treat any departure as permissible only on a narrow, necessity-based justification shown on the record. Coy held that a physical barrier preventing the witness from seeing the defendant is an obvious confrontation violation absent an individualized necessity showing, and Craig reaffirmed that the “requisite finding of necessity must of course be a case-specific one” based on evidence that this particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence. Here, the screen appears to have been used because Mississippi law mandated it rather than because the trial judge made the case-specific, evidence-based finding Craig requires; generalized legislative assumptions about trauma are beside the point. Given that this is a direct conflict with Coy/Craig’s procedural prerequisite for denying face-to-face confrontation, I would find a Confrontation Clause violation on these facts.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The baseline Confrontation Clause rule guarantees face-to-face confrontation at trial, and Coy and Craig recognize only a narrow, case-specific necessity exception for child-witness shielding procedures. On this record, the trial court appears to have employed the screen because Mississippi law mandated it (or upon the prosecutor’s request), without an individualized, on-the-record finding—grounded in evidence about this particular child—that she would be unable to testify or would suffer serious trauma from seeing the defendant and that the screen was necessary to prevent that harm. That is precisely the kind of generalized, legislatively presumed justification Coy rejected and Craig conditioned away, and cross-examination and jury observation, while important, do not substitute for the required necessity finding when the State seeks to depart from face-to-face confrontation. Because the State is the proponent of the departure from the constitutional baseline and did not carry its burden to fit within Craig’s narrow exception, the procedure violated the Confrontation Clause on these facts.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Confrontation Clause permits a trial court to place a screen between a child witness and the defendant without making a case-specific, evidence-based finding that this particular child needs that procedure to prevent trauma and ensure reliable testimony.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. VI (Confrontation Clause), as applied through Coy v. Iowa and Maryland v. Craig; also implicated is Mississippi’s mandatory child-witness screen procedure (cited as Miss. Code Ann. § 99-43-101(2)(g)) and Mississippi Rule of Evidence 803(25) (tender-years hearsay exception) as background to the hearing described.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Pitts argues that using a screen that blocked his four-year-old daughter’s view of him violated the Sixth Amendment because the trial court treated the screening procedure as mandatory and failed to make the constitutionally required, case-specific finding of necessity supported by evidence that this particular child would suffer trauma from face-to-face confrontation; he contends the Mississippi decision conflicts with Coy (which rejects generalized or legislatively presumed trauma) and Craig (which allows departures from face-to-face confrontation only after individualized necessity findings), making the error structural or at least not harmless and warranting summary reversal.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Mississippi argues the trial satisfied the essential elements of confrontation (oath, cross-examination, and jury observation) and that the trial court determined the screen procedure was necessary to protect the child from trauma; in any event, the State contends any error was harmless because independent evidence—including other witnesses’ testimony, the child’s statements to authorities, and a videotaped forensic interview—overwhelmingly established guilt, and the child’s forensic interview video was properly considered in the harmless-error analysis (including because it was introduced by the defense).
key_precedents: Ohio v. Roberts, 448 U.S. 56 (1980) (abrogated in part by Crawford v. Washington)
Little v. State, 72 So. 3d 557 (Miss. Ct. App. 2011)
Lambert v. State, 101 So. 3d 1172 (Miss. Ct. App. 2012)
New Orleans & N.E.R. Co. v. Weary, 217 So. 2d 274 (Miss. 1968)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument is that oath, cross-examination, and the jury’s ability to observe demeanor preserve the core of confrontation even if a screen blocks face-to-face contact. But as Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Alito emphasize, those safeguards are necessary but not sufficient under Craig: before dispensing with face-to-face confrontation, the trial court must make an individualized, evidence-based necessity finding that this particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence and that the measure is necessary. Coy treats a physical screen as a paradigmatic deprivation, and the record here appears to reflect an effectively categorical use of the screen without the required case-specific gatekeeping determination. The appropriate course is to reverse or vacate and remand for application of the correct Craig framework rather than allow general reliability arguments to substitute for the missing threshold finding.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Respondent’s strongest contention is that oath, cross-examination, and the jury’s observation provide the functional substance of confrontation even if the child cannot see the accused. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito explain, Coy treats a physical barrier as an obvious deprivation of face-to-face confrontation, and Craig allows that departure only after an individualized, evidence-based necessity finding that this particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence and that the accommodation is necessary. Those procedural safeguards are therefore necessary but not sufficient; they cannot substitute for Craig’s threshold gatekeeping. Because the record reflects no case-specific finding and suggests the screen was used categorically or effectively as a default, the State has not brought this case within Craig’s narrow exception.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The State’s best point is that the child testified under oath, was cross-examined, and was visible to the jury—features Craig treated as critical to reliability. But as the Chief Justice explains, those safeguards are not a substitute for Craig’s threshold requirement: an individualized, evidence-based finding that this particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence and that the screen was necessary. Coy makes a physical screen an “obvious” confrontation burden, and allowing its categorical or effectively mandatory use based on generalized assumptions would expand Craig’s narrow exception in a way the Sixth Amendment does not tolerate. I agree with Justice Kavanaugh that no “magic words” are required, but the record must still affirmatively show the required necessity determination, and it does not.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The State’s strongest claim—that protecting very young children is compelling and that oath, cross-examination, and jury observation preserve reliability—cannot do the constitutional work Craig assigns to a threshold, individualized necessity finding. As Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson emphasize, Craig’s sequencing matters: only after a court finds, on evidence, that this particular child would be traumatized by this defendant’s presence and that the screen is necessary may the State dispense with face-to-face confrontation. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh are also right that this is not about “magic words,” but the record must affirmatively show the judge actually made the required child-specific determination rather than treating the screen as effectively mandatory. Without that predicate, we risk normalizing confrontation-limiting measures for convenience and eroding a protection that matters most when liberty is at stake and the accused is least able to counter a credibility contest.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Respondent’s best point is that the child testified under oath, was cross-examined, and was visible to the jury—so confrontation’s functional safeguards were present. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh stress, Craig makes those safeguards necessary, not sufficient: before dispensing with face-to-face confrontation the trial court must make an individualized, evidence-based necessity finding tied to this child and to trauma from the defendant’s presence, not just the courtroom. Treating a screen as effectively mandatory under a statute flips Craig’s sequencing and replaces a constitutional prerequisite with a generalized assumption about children—precisely the kind of reliability-by-judicial (or legislative) say-so that the Confrontation Clause rejects. On this record, the missing predicate finding is dispositive, so I remain for reversal (or vacatur and remand) under the proper Craig framework.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The State’s strongest contention is that Craig tolerates a screen so long as oath, cross-examination, and demeanor evidence remain, making any defect here a mere failure to recite particular words. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh stress, Craig’s accommodation is not a free-floating balancing test; it is a narrow exception triggered only by an individualized, evidence-based finding that this child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence and that the measure is necessary. Coy rejects the legislature’s presumed necessity, and allowing a categorical practice here would untether the departure from any historically grounded baseline of face-to-face confrontation. The absence of an on-the-record necessity determination also reflects a gatekeeping failure that risks prejudicing the jury by implying dangerousness without demonstrated need, as Justice Alito notes.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The State’s strongest argument is that the oath, cross-examination, and jury observation preserved the core reliability functions of confrontation and that requiring an express finding would amount to a “magic words” rule. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito explain, Craig makes those safeguards necessary but not sufficient; the constitutional baseline is face-to-face confrontation, and departing from it requires a case-specific, evidence-based necessity determination tied to this particular child and the defendant’s presence. We can be pragmatic and avoid checklist formalism, but the record still must affirmatively show the trial court actually made the Craig predicate finding rather than applying a categorical or effectively mandatory practice. Because that predicate finding is missing here, the screen procedure cannot be upheld under Coy/Craig, and reversal (with any harmless-error analysis on remand under the proper framework) is warranted.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest respondent-side point is that the child testified under oath, was cross-examined, and was observed by the jury—so the functional reliability safeguards were present. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, those safeguards are not substitutes for Craig’s threshold requirement: an individualized, evidence-based finding that this particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence and that the screen was necessary. Coy treats a physical barrier blocking the witness’s view of the accused as an obvious departure from the face-to-face baseline, and the record here does not show the trial court actually performed the constitutionally required analysis rather than relying on generalized assumptions or statutory availability. Given that doctrinal sequencing, the absence of on-the-record Craig findings is dispositive on this record, irrespective of how much cross-examination occurred.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Respondent’s best contention—that the legislature’s general judgment about trauma to very young children, plus oath/cross/jury observation, suffices—misframes Craig by treating those reliability safeguards as a substitute for (rather than conditions following) the threshold necessity finding. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Craig’s sequencing matters: the court must first make an individualized, evidence-based determination that this particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence (not the courtroom generally) and that the screen is necessary, or else the procedure becomes the kind of categorical exception Coy warned would erode the confrontation baseline. Justice Barrett’s observation that the record suggests the screen operated as effectively mandatory underscores that the constitutional defect is the missing gatekeeping finding, which cannot be cured post hoc by pointing to other trial safeguards. Because the State seeks to expand a narrow, defendant-protective carveout into a routine option, I would reverse (or vacate and remand) for application of the proper Craig framework on an adequate record.

John Roberts.reasoning: Coy and Craig supply the controlling test, and it is not satisfied by a categorical or effectively mandatory use of a screen for child witnesses: the trial court must first make a case-specific, evidence-based finding that this particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence (not merely by the courtroom generally) and that the special measure is necessary while preserving adversarial testing. Here, the procedure appears to have been treated as required under Mississippi’s scheme rather than preceded by the individualized necessity determination Craig demands, which is precisely the sort of threshold finding a court must make before authorizing an exception that burdens a core procedural guarantee. Because the lower court’s analysis rests on an assumption that a screen may be used without the requisite circumstance-specific findings, the proper course is to vacate or reverse and require compliance with Craig’s prerequisites rather than allowing general interests in child protection to substitute for the demanded factfinding.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause’s text contemplates a “face-to-face” encounter with the witnesses against the accused, and our decisions in Coy and Craig treat any departure from that ordinary practice as a narrow exception that must be justified by a case-specific, evidence-based finding of necessity. Here, the trial court treated Mississippi’s screen procedure as effectively mandatory and did not make the individualized finding—after hearing evidence—that this particular four-year-old would be traumatized by Pitts’ presence and that the screen was necessary to secure her testimony. Because the screen was designed to prevent the child from seeing the defendant, it implicates the core confrontation interest identified in Coy, and Craig permits such a measure only upon the required particularized showing. On this record, the State cannot substitute generalized legislative assumptions or post hoc harmlessness arguments for the constitutionally required finding that must precede denying face-to-face confrontation.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Sixth Amendment’s text guarantees a right “to be confronted with the witnesses against” the accused, and Coy held that placing a screen to block a witness’s view of the defendant is an especially “obvious” denial of face-to-face confrontation absent a particularized justification. Craig permits a departure from face-to-face confrontation only when the trial court makes an individualized, evidence-based finding that this particular child needs the procedure to avoid trauma that would impair the child’s ability to testify, and the record here reflects the trial court treated the screen as effectively mandatory rather than making that case-specific necessity determination. Although I am attentive to the practical realities of protecting child witnesses and do not view confrontation as absolute, Craig’s narrow exception is the controlling rule, and a generalized or legislatively presumed need cannot substitute for the constitutionally required finding. Because the screening procedure went to the core confrontation interest and was imposed without the predicate findings Craig demands, the Confrontation Clause was violated on these facts.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause’s face-to-face requirement may be relaxed to protect a child, but only after a trial court makes a case-specific, evidence-based finding that this particular child would suffer trauma from seeing the defendant and that the accommodation is necessary while preserving adversarial testing. Here, the court treated the screen as effectively mandatory and did not make the individualized necessity finding Coy and Craig require, substituting a generalized assumption about young children for evidence about the child before it—an approach that risks both unfairness to the accused and unreliable factfinding. Protecting vulnerable child witnesses is an important public policy, but fairness demands a tailored showing and a careful record so courts do not normalize confrontation-limiting measures without necessity. On these facts, the constitutional error is the absence of the required finding, and the judgment should be reversed so any protective procedure is supported by the individualized record Craig demands.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause’s core guarantee is face-to-face, adversarial testing of accusation, and Coy and Craig make clear that a court may dispense with that element for a child witness only after a case-specific, evidence-based finding that this particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence and that the special procedure is necessary. Here, the trial court treated the screen as effectively mandatory (or at least as available on request) and did not make the individualized necessity finding Craig requires, so the State did not carry its constitutional burden to justify the departure from confrontation. Nor can the error be saved by generalized assurances that oath, cross-examination, and observation occurred; Craig allows the exception only on an adequate record showing necessity as to this child, not as a categorical rule. And to the extent Mississippi relies on the child’s out-of-court forensic interview or similar statements in harmlessness, that invites the very Confrontation Clause mistake my approach rejects—using uncross-examined testimonial accusations for their truth to paper over a denial of the constitutionally prescribed mode of reliability testing.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Sixth Amendment’s confrontation right, as the people fixed it, guarantees face-to-face confrontation absent a historically grounded exception (or a close analogue), and this Court’s cases allow departure only on an individualized showing of necessity. Here, the trial court appears to have treated Mississippi’s screen procedure as effectively mandatory or categorical, employing it without a case-specific, evidence-based finding that this particular four-year-old could not reasonably testify in the defendant’s presence without trauma of the sort Craig requires. That unexplained, legislatively presumed necessity is exactly what Coy forbids, and it also risks distorting the jury’s factfinding by presenting testimony under a special procedure without an on-the-record showing that the measure was needed and narrowly tailored. On these facts, the Confrontation Clause was violated because the State did not justify this modern deviation from face-to-face confrontation with the required individualized necessity finding.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Coy and Craig do not impose a rigid “magic-words” script, but they do require that the record affirmatively show a case-specific, evidence-based finding that this particular child needs a departure from face-to-face confrontation. Here, as described, the trial court treated Mississippi’s screen provision as effectively mandatory and did not make (or did not base on evidence) the individualized necessity determination Craig demands, which is precisely the kind of legislatively presumed trauma Coy forbids. Respecting state procedural flexibility does not extend to dispensing with Craig’s core prerequisite before using a physical barrier that blocks the witness’s view of the defendant. Given that face-to-face confrontation is the default constitutional rule and the record does not show the required individualized finding, I would vote to reverse (leaving harmlessness to be assessed under the proper Confrontation Clause framework on remand if necessary).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Coy and Craig treat face-to-face confrontation as the constitutional baseline and allow a departure only after a trial court makes a case-specific, evidence-based finding that this particular child cannot reasonably testify in the defendant’s presence without trauma that would impair the truth-seeking function. On this record, the screen appears to have been treated as effectively mandatory upon the State’s request, without the individualized necessity determination that Craig requires; generalized assumptions about child-witness distress, or reliance on ordinary evidentiary practices, cannot substitute for the Sixth Amendment finding. While trial courts receive deference on case-management when they make reasoned determinations supported by evidence, deference presupposes that the court actually performed the constitutional analysis Craig demands. Because the procedure here blocked the child’s view of the defendant absent the requisite on-the-record necessity finding, the judgment cannot stand on the theory that oath, cross-examination, and jury observation alone suffice to cure the specific face-to-face deprivation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The baseline Sixth Amendment rule, as Coy underscores, is that confrontation ordinarily entails face-to-face encounter, and Craig permits departure only as a narrow, defendant-protective exception that must be justified by a case-specific, evidence-based finding of necessity. On this record, the trial court treated the screen as effectively mandatory under Mississippi’s statute and did not make the individualized determination Craig requires that this particular four-year-old could not reasonably testify in petitioner’s presence without trauma that would impair reliable testimony. That sequencing matters: once the constitutional problem is established (denial of face-to-face confrontation without the requisite findings), the State cannot “cure” it by pointing to general indicia of confrontation (oath, cross-examination, jury observation) or by invoking other inculpatory evidence, because those considerations do not supply the missing Craig necessity finding. Given the centrality of the child’s in-court testimony and the heightened risk that formal safeguards will not realistically offset the prejudice from a procedure that signals danger and credibility, I would reverse (or at minimum vacate and remand) for application of the proper Craig/Coy framework rather than allowing the exception to swallow the default rule.
